questions.problem:
$$
f(y,z)=⟨\text{___},\,y,\,z⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(y,z)$ above parametrizes the parabolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as $8{z}^{2}=x.$ What is the first component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
For any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨8{z}^{2},\,y,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $y\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $8{z}^{2}.$

questions.problem:
$$
f(t,y)=⟨\text{_____},y,\,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(t,y)$ above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as $4{x}^{2}+25{z}^{2}=100.$ What is the first component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the ellipse 

$$
4{x}^{2}+25{z}^{2}=100\,⟹\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}=1
$$

in $xz$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,z⟩=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ),
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4} & =\frac{(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}{4} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t,y) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,2\pi )$ and $y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

questions.problem:
$$
f(x,t)=⟨x,\,\text{_____},\,7\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

The vector-valued function $f(x,t)$ above parametrizes one sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as ${y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=49$ for $y\ge 7.$ What is the second component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the hyperbola ${y}^{2}-{z}^{2}=49$ for $y\ge 7$ in $yz$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨y,z⟩=⟨7\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,7\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{sec}⁡t)^{2}-(7\operatorname{tan}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =49{sec}^{2}⁡t-49{tan}^{2}⁡t \\  & =49({sec}^{2}⁡t-{tan}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,t) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨x,\,7\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,7\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})$ and $x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $7\operatorname{sec}⁡t.$

questions.problem:
$$
f(t,y)=⟨\text{_____},\,y,\,2\operatorname{sec}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

The vector-valued function $f(t,y)$ above parametrizes one sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as ${z}^{2}-{x}^{2}=4$ for $z\ge 2.$ What is the first component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the hyperbola ${z}^{2}-{x}^{2}=4$ for $z\ge 2$ in $xz$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,z⟩=⟨2\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sec}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =(2\operatorname{sec}⁡t)^{2}-(2\operatorname{tan}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =4{sec}^{2}⁡t-4{tan}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4({sec}^{2}⁡t-{tan}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t,y) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y,\,2\operatorname{sec}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})$ and $y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$

questions.problem:
$$
f(t,y)=⟨\text{_____},\,y,\,4\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

The vector-valued function $f(t,y)$ above parametrizes one sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as ${x}^{2}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{16}=1$ for $x\ge 1.$ What is the first component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the hyperbola ${x}^{2}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{16}=1$ for $x\ge 1$ in $xz$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,z⟩=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{16} & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡t)^{2}-\frac{(4\operatorname{tan}⁡t)^{2}}{16} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡t-\frac{16{tan}^{2}⁡t}{16} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡t-{tan}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t,y) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,y,\,4\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})$ and $y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $\operatorname{sec}⁡t.$

questions.problem:
$$
f(t,z)=⟨3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,\text{_____},\,z⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

The vector-valued function $f(t,z)$ above parametrizes one sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as $2{x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}=18$ for $x\ge 3.$ What is the second component of $f?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the hyperbola

$$
2{x}^{2}-9{y}^{2}=18\,⇒\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=1
$$

for $x\ge 3$ in $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,y⟩=⟨3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & =\frac{(3\operatorname{sec}⁡t)^{2}}{9}-\frac{(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t)^{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{9{sec}^{2}⁡t}{9}-\frac{2{tan}^{2}⁡t}{2} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡t-{tan}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})$ and $z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $\sqrt{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$

canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\mathbf{f}(t,z) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: 4\sin{t}, \: z \big\rangle
$$

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(t,z)$ above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1.$ What is the first component of $\mathbf{f}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1$ in $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
\langle x,y \rangle = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 4\sin{t} \big\rangle,
\qquad t \in [0,2\pi),
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}{16} \\  & =\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡t}{4}+\frac{16{sin}^{2}⁡t}{16} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in [0,2\pi)$ and $z \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}2\cos{t}}.$

canonical_examples.problem:

$$

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(t,y)$ above parametrizes one sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\dfrac{z^2}{4} - \dfrac{x^2}{16} = 1$ for $z \geq 2.$ What is the third component of $\mathbf{f}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the hyperbola $\dfrac{z^2}{4} - \dfrac{x^2}{16} = 1$ for $z \geq 2$ in $xz$-plane has the parametrization

$$
\langle x , z \rangle = \big \langle 4\tan{t}, \, 2\sec{t} \big\rangle,

\qquad t \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{(2\operatorname{sec}⁡t)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(4\operatorname{tan}⁡t)^{2}}{16} \\  & =\frac{4{sec}^{2}⁡t}{4}-\frac{16{tan}^{2}⁡t}{16} \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡t-{tan}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t,y) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y,\,2\operatorname{sec}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and $y \in (-\infty, \infty).$

Therefore, the third component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}2\sec{t}}.$
